Trump will meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for talks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this week in China’s Shenzhen, the White House confirmed. Top of the agenda for Washington and Moscow is the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START) , which lapsed in February, marking the end of more than half a century of limits on US and Russian strategic nuclear weapons. Trump previously rejected Russia’s proposal to extend the treaty, demanding instead a “new, improved and modernised” deal that includes Beijing. But China has long signalled that it is not ready to join any nuclear arms control treaty. New START was a treaty signed in 2010 by then-US President Barack Obama and Dmitry Medvedev, a close ally of Vladimir Putin who served as Russia’s president from 2008 to 2012. It was extended in 2021 for an additional five years when Joe Biden was the US president. Under the agreement, Russia and the US were permitted to deploy no more than 1,550 strategic nuclear warheads and a maximum of 700 long-range missiles and bombers, had to impose a limit of 800 intercontinental ballistic missiles in deployment and grant permission for up to 18 inspections of strategic nuclear weapons sites annually by the other party. New START collapsed in February after the five-year extension lapsed. This key accord was in turn built from earlier arms control treaties signed between Washington and Moscow. The first of those, START I, was signed in 1991 between the US and the Soviet Union in the dying days of the Cold War. It remained in place until 2009 with the aim of capping US and Russian strategic nuclear arsenals. START II, its successor, aimed to further reduce the number of deployed strategic nuclear warheads in addition to removing multiwarhead intercontinental ballistic missiles altogether. It was signed in 1993 but never came into force. Russia formally withdrew from it in 2002. Known as The Godfather or the "Boss of Bosses", Félix Gallardo was the head of the all-powerful Guadalajara Cartel, which reigned over Mexican drug trafficking at the height of the cocaine boom of the 1980s. At the time, it created a new modus operandi in the illegal drug trade which endures to this day. He had been in state custody since 1989. The name Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo will echo through the annals of drug-trafficking history more than any other except perhaps Pablo Escobar's. He led the organisation which revolutionised drug smuggling in the region by entering into partnership with the Colombian cartels, particularly Escobar's Medellín Cartel, to combine production in the Andes with Mexican transportation across the border into the United States. At one point an estimated 80% of all cocaine that entered the US came from the Medellín Cartel. Félix Gallardo and his organisation played a major role in smuggling it in. At its height, the Guadalajara Cartel under Félix Gallardo exerted huge influence over Mexican politics and law enforcement, controlling entire police networks and state governorships. In 1985, the net started to tighten around the leaders of the cartel following the torture and murder of a DEA agent, Enrique "Kiki" Camarena. Camarena had angered them after he had discovered and then destroyed a vast marijuana plantation in Chihuahua, which belonged to the criminal group. His murder sparked one of the biggest manhunts the US government has ever launched in North America. In 1989, Félix Gallardo was captured and sentenced to decades in prison. In ill health, he was granted house arrest in 2022 but technical problems with electronic ankle monitoring prevented his transfer. He died in hospital in his native Guadalajara. clusters.text: The fire is the second blaze in Thailand to cause mass casualties since July. A fire in ⁠a commercial ⁠building on Thailand’s southern resort island of Phuket has ⁠killed at least 11 people and injured 16 others, according to police. The blaze in the tourist hub of Patong started at about 3:17am on Monday (20:17 GMT on Sunday) in a building housing a restaurant, rented accommodation and a motorcycle rental shop, and later spread to several other buildings nearby. Phuket police commander Surachai Sooksai said officers are still investigating the cause of the fire, but an initial investigation found that an electrical transformer near the building had exploded shortly before the fire started, ruling out arson. Phuket Governor Chodnarin Koedsom said the rental shop had about 100 motorcycles, along with stored gas, engine oil, plastic materials and tyres. He said these combustible materials may have contributed to the rapid spread of the fire and the thick, toxic smoke. Of the 16 people injured, the authorities said, 15 were Thai and one was a Myanmar national, adding that no tourists were among those injured or killed. The injured were treated at a hospital for smoke inhalation and injuries from broken glass. Thailand’s approach to health and safety regulations, especially in bars and nightclubs has long raised concerns. In July, a crowded bar in the capital, Bangkok, was engulfed in flames and smoke, killing about 40 people after an electrical short circuit triggered the blaze, authorities said. Four people were killed and many more injured in a fire that swept through a club popular with tourists on Phuket in 2012. clusters.text: The second seat at Red Bull Racing has long been viewed as one of the most high-pressure environments in Formula 1. While the Milton Keynes operation frequently cycled through highly rated prospects trying to find a match for Max Verstappen, former team principal Christian Horner is now openly questioning the logic of that ruthless driver pipeline. Speaking on the High Performance podcast, Horner reflected on his tenure managing the team and admitted that he frequently disagreed with how quickly drivers were thrown into the deep end against a generational talent. "Some of these drivers were arriving too soon, and I didn't completely agree with the speed at which they were arriving into Red Bull Racing, but there was a determination to have them from the Red Bull Junior pool," Horner revealed. Horner named Pierre Gasly, Alex Albon, and Liam Lawson as prime examples of prospects who were rushed into the senior seat before they were properly prepared. One example of this developmental failure was Pierre Gasly's short-lived stint with the senior team in 2019. Promoted after just one full season at sister outfit Toro Rosso (now Racing Bulls), Gasly struggled to adapt to the highly sensitive Red Bull chassis and the immense pressure of Verstappen's raw pace. Horner recalled the exact moment the team watched the French driver's confidence collapse. During both the Austrian and Hungarian Grand Prix that year, Verstappen's pace was so blisteringly fast that he lapped Gasly on track. Pierre Gasly, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Jerry Andre / Motorsport Images "You could visibly see that they were feeling that pressure, whether it was Pierre, I remember [him] getting lapped in Austria and at the Hungarian Grand Prix two races in a row, and he was broken in those races," Horner stated. Immediately following the Hungarian Grand Prix, Red Bull abruptly demoted Gasly back to Toro Rosso for the remainder of the season, replacing him with Albon. While Horner noted that the Red Bull system usually provided a "parachute" by allowing drivers to return to the junior team rather than firing them completely, he did not shy away from criticising the harsh reality of the environment. "It was, on the one hand, hugely generous what Red Bull were doing, but it was quite brutal in terms of its execution that you were the flavour of the month until you weren't," Horner concluded.

The triumvirate of the RBI, the administrator, and YES Bank, in conducting the entire affair of dealing with the bonds worth more than Rs 8,415 crore, to put it mildly, is questionable, the court had observed.The bench also held that an administrator appointed under the Banking Regulation Act effectively takes the place of a bank's board of directors and cannot assume regulatory powers vested with the RBI.Any action beyond the authority conferred on the administrator, the court said, would be illegal and void.Also read: SBI helped save YES Bank, Japan came aboard, and now an ₹8,415-crore ghost is crashing its comebackWhat is the YES Bank AT1 bond case?The dispute dates back to March 2020, when the RBI orchestrated a rescue of YES Bank after the private lender ran into a severe financial crisis amid allegations of malfeasance, fraud and wrongdoing.As part of the restructuring, a consortium of banks, led by the State Bank of India (SBI), was brought in to infuse equity into the lender.
